berate

/bih-RAYT/ - rhymes with crate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Berate means to scold loudly and at length.

The bus driver berated the fare-jumper all the way to the next stop, and the whole bus rode in silence.

Worked Example

When the caterer arrived an hour late, the bride's father berated him in the hotel lobby until the manager steered them both into an office.

Berate means to scold loudly and at length — both parts matter. A chide is a sentence and a scolding is a minute, but a berating fills the room and keeps going; the listener stands there while it rolls over them.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

excoriate: To excoriate is to flay someone with savage criticism, and it is most at home in print — reviews, reports, and editorials excoriate. Berate is spoken and face-to-face, and volume and duration are its signature: the listener stands there while it rolls over them. Critics excoriate; furious coaches berate.

rebuke: A rebuke is sharp disapproval delivered sternly and briefly — one cutting sentence can be a rebuke, and then it is over. Berate runs the other way: loud, sustained, a scolding that fills the room and keeps going. A rebuke is a slap of words; berating is a storm of them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

applaud: express loud approval of someone

congratulate: tell someone you admire their success

Where it sits · how loud and long the telling-off runs — nag → scold → berate

nag vs. berate: Nagging pesters in small, repeated doses — it never rises to berate's sustained roar.

scold vs. berate: A scolding is sharp but brief; it stops short of berate, which is loud and keeps going.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — be-

Prefix — be-: thoroughly, all over

Root — rate

Root — rate: to scold (an old English verb, now vanished)

Put it together

Put it together: Be- (thoroughly) + rate (an old verb meaning to scold) = to scold thoroughly. The scolding rate survives nowhere else in modern English — today's rate, 'to score or rank,' is an unrelated Latin word — so berate is a fossil: the last home of a dead verb.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Berate keeps an extinct English verb alive: rate once meant 'to scold angrily' all by itself. That rate died out around Shakespeare's time, leaving berate no living relatives — the rate on a menu or a report card comes from Latin ratus and is no kin at all.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / vivid

Berate is the loud, sustained, face-to-face scolding — pick it when volume and duration are the point. Its unit-mates scale neatly: chide (gentle), admonish (firm, measured), chastise (severe, official), berate (loud and long). A tirade, meanwhile, is the speech itself, not the act of aiming it at someone.
